quote: Have no doubt about it, when people annoy and torment you when you are doing the right thing, those people are the lackeys of the wickedest sinner of all. They are slaves of the author of every evil deed. David saw this with prophetic eyes and recognized the face of the evil one. So he kept quiet. He had no wish whatever to do the will of the evil one. So he kept quiet. He had no wish whatever to do the will of him who ruins one's peace of mind. He simply said nothing. He closed his doors in silence; patience lay before him, and silence kept a sleepless vigil. No enemy could creep in, and from his cloistered lips no ambivalent speech, no heedless talk, could issue forth. Mightier far is the patient person who can govern himself than the valiant one who captures citadels. The just person is his own cloister; he is his own eternal guard.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue" [Psalm 39:1]. ...For it is not without reason that the tongue is set in a moist place, but because it is so prone to slip. Perceiving therefore how hard it was for a man to be under the necessity of speaking, and not to say something that he will wish unsaid, and filled with disgust at these sins, he seeks to avoid the like. To this difficulty is he exposed who is seeking to "leap beyond."... Although I have "leaped beyond" the pleasures of earth, although the fleeting passions for things temporal ensnare me not, though now I despise these things below, and am rising up to better things than these, yet in these very better things the satisfaction of knowledge in the sight of God is enough for me. Of what use is it for me to speak what is to be laid hold of, and to give a handle to cavillers? Therefore, "I said, I will…

"I said" [has] the sense, "I determined," his meaning being, I determined within myself not to sin against my oppressor simply in action but also not to say anything against him by word of mouth, especially since what is initially verbal abuse turns to physical abuse, and the person who is determined not to do physical harm ought not have recourse to verbal abuse.

Just as one man advances according to God, and by applying zeal to himself becomes better than his former self, so also it used to happen to the whole people. And on this account, as it too advanced, there came to it also an increase of the law. In short, just as it is written in the law, there are certain precepts for the priests and Levites concerning sacrifices and the other solemn observances: yet when the people advanced, at that time when there was still in it the power of advancing, the matter did not stand still in that first order, but there were bound to those men certain more eminent legislations, a second and a third. And if anyone wishes to know what these things are that were added concerning the priests and Levites, let him read the first book of Chronicles, and let him patiently examine that whole catalogue of names, and he will find there a certain admirable order and a…

But now let us at last see what the voice of the righteous man utters, and, seeing ourselves as though in a mirror, let us look at ourselves, whether we can be such, or whether much is lacking to us, or whether indeed we are now near, although we have not yet fully attained. Since therefore the beginning of many sins is human speech, and our mouth serves many evils, and it is very difficult to find a man who, for even one hour at least, keeps his mouth and his tongue from sin, he says: "I said: I will keep my ways, that I sin not with my tongue". I said to my very self, and I spoke within myself, and I added these things: Thus I wish to keep my ways, that I sin not; in this way I can keep them, if I guard my tongue. "For by thy words", he says, "thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned". And again: "Amen I say to you, for every idle word you shall render an…

In these events one may understand as fulfilled the prophecy which says: "while the sinner stood against me, I was made dumb and was humbled and kept silent from good things", so that that sinner foretold in these words may be understood to be Caiaphas, who stood against Jesus. At the same time we learn also from this passage to despise the voices of slanderers and false witnesses, so that we neither hold them worthy of our reply, nor defend our own selves where the things said against us are not consistent. For what need is there to resist those who resist themselves by saying things contrary to themselves? Especially where it is a greater thing freely and bravely to be silent than to defend oneself without any profit, so that we may not be humbled by false witnesses and wicked slanderers.

It is a universal custom to be upset when you see your plans at the mercy of sinners, and to be upset also at your own misfortunes, especially when you are badly treated by wrongdoers while conscious of your own virtuous behavior. The general run of people react to such developments by turning to criticism and displeasure with the God of all. Hence, blessed David says, "I shall guard my ways so as not to sin with my tongue": I kept my words to myself, that is, I made a decision and judgment to guard myself against any sin.

If you know there is sin, be silent. Do not add to your guilt by denying it. If you are not aware of sin, be silent. You are secure in your innocence. The reports of other people cannot nail any sin to a conscience that knows itself to be innocent.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "I became deaf, and was humbled, I held my peace from good" (ver. 2). For this person, who is "leaping beyond," suffers some difficulty in a certain stage to which he hath already attained; and he desires to advance beyond, even from thence, to avoid this difficulty. I was afraid of committing a sin; so that I spoke not; that I imposed on myself the necessity of silence: for I had spoken thus, "I will take heed to my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue." Whilst I was too much afraid of saying anything wrong, I kept silence from all that is good. For whence could I say good things, except that I heard them? "It is Thou that shalt make me to hear of joy and gladness." And the "friend of the bridegroom standeth and heareth Him, and rejoiceth on account of the bridegroom's voice," not his own. That he may speak true things, he hears what he is to say. For it is he that "speaketh a lie,"…

In temptation, good words flee from us and the spirit is silent. The soul speaks about those temptations that it recognizes and is silent about those it does not. In this place "good" indicates the virtues and knowledge that flee in the time of temptation.

When he was silent he ceased from good, that is, from the meditation of the Law, which is the teacher of good. When the grief of the sin renewed, the wound from sin became more serious, as when we lead others from meditation on the Law. It becomes a festering sore, having applied no medicine from divine precepts. And so he has not stood in silence, but when he had returned to his senses, he cast out that very thing bringing such harm to his spirit. He shows this by "my heart grew hot."

If insults are offered to you or to anyone else, or wrongs done, be immovable, and as far as an answer in retaliation is concerned, be silent "as one that is dumb," always singing in your heart this verse of the psalmist.

But since we sin most of all at that time, when the sinner stands against us, instigating and provoking us to send forth from our mouth something such as would hold us guilty in the future judgment, the holy Prophet, describing this, says: "While the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". Whenever the sinner stood against me and spoke ill of me, and disparaged and irritated me to render him the like, and to bring forth from my mouth things equal to his, I at that time meditated silence, so as to answer nothing at all. Therefore he says: "While the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". But we sometimes, if we are unwilling to be humbled, think other things and say within ourselves: What is this? This man has held me in contempt and has dared to thrust such things in my face, and thus to…

And what did he add to these things? "And my sorrow", he says, "was renewed". Those who in the struggle of the contest engage in mutual blows against one another always try to prepare themselves in these things, so that they may bravely bear the blows inflicted on them by their adversaries, and not receive the sense of pain, and this is for them the highest excellence: to sustain the strokes of arms or of heels without pain. Among these, that man is more perfect who, at the stroke of the wound, receives no sting of pain. But the second is he who indeed feels pain, but by no means yields to the pains. Understand something of this sort also in ourselves, when we are cursed, and the antagonist stands against us; if indeed we are well instructed, and strengthened in mind by long meditation, we are in no way at all grieved by the curses or reproaches inflicted, but by reason of the exceeding…

"And while I was musing, the fire burned" [Psalm 39:3]....I reflected on the words of my Lord, "Thou wicked and slothful servant, you ought to have put My money to the exchangers, and I at My coming should receive it again with usury." [Matthew 25:26-27] And that which follows may God avert from those who are His stewards! Bind him hand and foot, and let him be cast into outer darkness; [Matthew 25:30] the servant, who was not a waster of his master's goods, so as to destroy them, but was slothful in laying them out to improve them. What ought they to expect, who have wasted them in luxury, if they are condemned who through slothfulness have kept them? "As I was musing, the fire burned." And as he was in this state of wavering suspense, between speaking and holding his peace, between those who are prepared to cavil and those who are anxious to be instructed,...in this state of suspense,…

Whence therefore will you burn? Whence will "coals of fire" be found in you, who are never set on fire by the word of the Lord, never inflamed by the words of the Holy Spirit? Hear also elsewhere David himself saying: "my heart grew warm within me, and in my meditation a fire blazes forth". Whence do you grow warm? Whence is fire kindled in you, who never meditate on the divine words — nay, what is more unhappy, you grow warm at the spectacles of the circus, you grow warm at the contests of horses, at the struggle of athletes? And that fire is not from the altar of the Lord, but is that which is called "strange fire".

In what follows he still further describes the passion of the one who advances, when he says: "My heart grew hot within me". For when one hears the voice of the evil-speaker and the detractor, he cannot be without sorrow, like that man who is perfect, who by long-continued constancy has already merited blessedness: but this man feels pain, and feeling pain, with his heart growing hot, boils within himself and is troubled, yet not to such a degree as also to bring forth a word with a troubled heart, but he indeed grows hot in his inner parts, moved by the indignity of the matter, yet he boils away the flames of his heat through silence.

Let us see also another saying of the righteous man, which too with the utmost zeal we ought to be jealous to emulate. "And in my meditation a fire shall blaze forth". I too meditate upon the words of the Lord, and I frequently exercise myself in them, but I do not know whether I am such that in my meditation, from each single word of God, a fire proceeds, and kindles my heart, and inflames my soul to observe the things that I meditate. I too now speak the words of God, but I would wish that first in my own heart, and secondly also in the minds of the hearers, they might blaze forth: just as were those words which Jesus spoke, of which those who had heard said: "Was not our heart burning within us when on the way he opened to us the Scriptures"? Would that now too, as we open the divine Scriptures, our heart might grow hot within us, and in our meditation a fire be kindled, and we be…

It is not that he was enquiring about his own death—death is not the end of one who will rise again—but rather his enquiry concerned that end of which the apostle speaks: "Afterwards there will be the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father". … Evil will fade to nothingness, and eternal good will take its place.… That, surely, is the true end. It is not the end of one person alone, but the end of all. Why then does David say "my end"? But consider a moment who it is that is speaking. He speaks as humankind or as one representing men and sharing the same substance as they; he is one who stands for all, is in the likeness of all and is truly versed in that perfection that belongs to the consummate man.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "Lord, make me to know mine end" [Psalm 39:4]. For some things I have passed by already; and I have arrived at a certain point, and that to which I have arrived is better than that from which I have advanced to this; but yet there remains a point, which has to be left behind. For we are not to remain here, where there are trials, offenses, where we have to bear with persons who listen to us and cavil at us. "Make me to know mine end;" the end, from which I am still removed, not the course which is already before me.

Not even all the possessions amassed nor all humankind, if measured by their lifetime, from Adam to the last human being—not even this measure is anything in comparison with the measure of your life, Lord.
The end of the rational nature is the understanding of the holy Trinity.

"I have spoken", he says, "with my tongue". Let us consider what he has spoken with his tongue: for it seems to me that through these things he indicates something mystical. He says therefore: "Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me". If, he says, thou hast made known my end to me, and hast made known to me how great is the number of my days, I shall be able through these things to know also that other thing, what is lacking to me. Or perhaps through these things this too will seem to be indicated, that just as there is some end of every art — for example, the end of building is to make a house; of ship-building, to construct a ship which can overcome the waves of the sea and bear the assaults of the winds; and of each art there is some such end, on account of which the art itself seems to have been devised: so…

God, who knows precisely the allotted days of each one of us, regards nothing as immeasurable. His knowledge embraces the measure of all things. To him nothing is beyond his understanding, nothing is unweighed, nothing is unmeasured, nothing is unnumbered. He says, "The very hairs of your head have been numbered." … We know that God is said to have measured the heavens with the palm of his hand22—the palm, from thumb to little finger, being the span by which a thing is measured and its length ascertained. Those who accept this reading understand that our days are measured or numbered, and in that sense they are short. However, the all-knowing God has measured, as we said above, and fully comprehends the very heavens.… The prophet's days are not short but great, for God has measured them with the same palm as that with which he measured the heavens.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "Behold, thou hast made my days old" (ver. 5). For these days are "waxing old." I long for new days "that never shall wax old," that I may say, "Old things have passed away; behold, things are become new." Already new in hope; then in reality. For though, in hope and in faith, made new already, how much do we even now do after our old nature! For we are not so completely "clothed upon" with Christ, as not to bear about with us anything derived from Adam. Observe that Adam is "waxing old" within us, and Christ is being "renewed" in us. "Though our outward man is perishing, yet is our inward man being renewed day by day." Therefore, while we fix our thoughts on sin, on mortality, on time, that is hastening by, on sorrow, and toil, and labour, on stages of life following each other in succession, and continuing not, passing on insensibly from infancy even to old age; whilst, I say, we fix…

The life of mortals is a hard cause. What else is it to be born here, except to enter into a laborious life? Of the greater future labor, the very crying of the infant is a witness. From this troublesome banquet no one excuses himself. We must drink what Adam has offered. We were made by the hands of truth, but because of sin, we were cast into days of vanity. We were made in the image of God, but we wore it down through the transgression of sin. Therefore, the psalm admonishes us about how we were made, and to where we have arrived.

Such, brothers, is our life, we whose existence is so transitory. Such is the game we play on earth: we do not exist, and we are born, and being born we are dissolved. We are a fleeting dream, an apparition without substance, the flight of a bird that passes, a ship that leaves no trace on the sea. We are dust, a vapor, the morning dew, a flower growing but a moment and withering in a moment. "A person's days are as grass: as the flower of the field, so shall he flourish." Beautifully has holy David meditated on our weakness … and he defines the days of a person as the measure of a span.
source_title: ON HIS BROTHER ST. CAESARIUS, ORATION 7:19

quote: And he adds: "Behold, thou hast set my days as old ones". In the Greek it is written, παλαιστάς, which signifies a measure of four fingers. Wishing therefore to teach us who now in this life lead brief and very few days, he spoke this verse of which we spoke above. From which it is understood that another too could say, that Thou hast set my days one finger, as following upon the brevity of time, and another two fingers or three. But I ask whether any of men can say, that My days are ten fingers, or twenty, or even more. And because we come upon difficult passages, I would wish to inquire whether somewhere in the Scriptures we find any such thing, from which that which seems obscure could be opened up more plainly. In Isaiah I remember it is written: "Who has measured", he says, "the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist"? From which let…

He also adds in what follows and says: "My substance is as nothing before thee". Unless he had added before thee, I should be greatly grieved, for the reason that he had said the human substance to be nothing. But now, because he said before thee, it is as if he said that in comparison indeed either with the angels or with the rest of the creatures, my substance is not abject, nor least. In short, even if we act well, and keep the commandments of the Lord, we are invited to the fellowship of the angels: "They shall be", he says, "as the angels of God in heaven". But in comparison with God, even if I be Peter, against whom the gates of hell shall not prevail, my substance before him is nothing. And he used sufficiently the proper term of nature. For all is nothing, however great it be, whatever is out of nothing, for he alone is the one who is, and who always is. But our substance is as…

But in what follows, as if explaining this very thing which he said, that "my substance is as nothing before thee", he added and says: "Nevertheless the whole is vanity, every living man". How do you take "living"? If indeed we think true life to be vanity, why do we labor? But see whether perhaps this which he says, every living man, is to be taken of this present life, as it is written, and we shall prove it by testimonies. For all things that are in this life among men are vain, even if Moses be in this life, for he too knows in part, and prophesies in part, and sees through a mirror and in an enigma, and knows a shadow, and is taught figures, and does not yet see the truth, and therefore he is indeed living, but his life is vanity. And do you wish to see that it is vanity? "When that which is perfect shall have come, those things which are in part shall be destroyed". But all that…

"Albeit man walketh in the Image" [Psalm 39:6]. In what "Image," save that of Him who said, "Let Us make man in Our Image, after Our Likeness." "Albeit man walks in the Image." For the reason he says "albeit," is, that this is some great thing. And this "albeit" is followed by "nevertheless," that the "albeit" which you have already heard, should relate to what is beyond the sun; but this "nevertheless," which is to follow, to what is "under the sun," and that the one should relate to the Truth, the other to "vanity." "Albeit," then, "that man walketh in the Image, nevertheless he is disquieted in vain." Hear the cause of his "disquieting," and see if it be not a vain one; that thou mayest trample it under foot, that thou mayest "leap beyond it," and mayest dwell on high, where that "vanity" is not. What "vanity" is that? "He heapeth up riches, and knoweth not for whom he may be…

"Although man walks about in an image". An image is necessarily the image of something. For Holy Scripture too, when it names an image, sometimes indeed defines it and says whose image it is, but sometimes sets down "image" without any qualification. Thus, concerning the Savior, when it says "who is the image", it did not keep silent whose image he is, but added, saying: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature". And again, when it teaches us about the diverse images, and that each single person bears some image, it says: "As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly". With a qualification—either "of the earthly" or "of the heavenly"—it named the image. But elsewhere it speaks without any qualification, just as in this place it says: "Although man walks about in an image". But in the image of what? Of God, or in the…

But this verse seems to me to contain also another mystery: that the life and manner of living in this world is a kind of imaginary thing and an image, while the future one will not be imaginary but true; and this is what is meant, that each person has an image of virtue, yet does not properly and sincerely live in the virtue itself. Now what we say is of this sort: Wisdom and knowledge are a great part of the virtues; but in the present life, if anyone thinks he has known, he has not yet known as he ought to know, for he who knows, knows in a riddle. Therefore we walk about in an image of knowledge and not in knowledge itself, through which one knows face to face. So likewise we walk about in the image of wisdom, and not yet in wisdom itself, because we do not yet behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. The same things I dare to say concerning the righteousness of God, that we…

There follows: "He treasures up, and knows not for whom he gathers these things". For it was necessary to inquire what those things are that are treasured up while it is unknown for whom they are gathered, and what those things are that are gathered while it is not unknown for whom they remain.

Our hope and our patience is Christ; he is our redemption; he is our expectation.… Look on us, Lord, when you come in judgment; let your mercy look on us.… In the power of your mercy lies the substance of our soul and life. We must not fear physical death; rather, we should fear him who can save or destroy our soul. Our soul's substance is that virtue that God has poured into hearts made in the image of himself.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "And now" [Psalm 39:7]. "And now," saith this Idithun,-looking back on a certain "vain" show, and looking up to a certain Truth, standing midway where he has something beyond him, and something also behind him, having below him the place from which he took his spring, having above him that toward which he has stretched forth;-"And now," when I have "over-leaped" some things, when I have trampled many things under foot, when I am no longer captivated by things temporal; even now, I am not perfect, "I have not yet apprehended." "For it is by hope that we are saved; but hope that is seen is not hope; for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it." Therefore he says: "And now what wait I for? Is it not for the Lord?" He is my expectation, who hath given me all those things, that I might despise them. He will give…
We will have to say that if we give in to troubles, we do not believe in him insofar as he is endurance; and if we are weak, we have not believed in him insofar as he is strength.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 19:157

quote: There follows: "And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?" As Christ is our wisdom, and Christ is righteousness, according to what is written: "Who was made wisdom for us from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption"; so also our expectation, that is, our patience, is Christ. Therefore let not the wise man glory in wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, because we have all things in Christ. And now therefore what is my expectation, that is, my patience? The Lord. "And my substance is from you". If I have a substance of spiritual riches, it is from God; "for God breathed into the face of man the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul".

It is not merely one lapse that he is confessing, for he prays to be forgiven all his iniquities. He knows that without God's forgiveness no one can be saved. For we were born in sin. We have inherited a stain. Our human condition has a congenital tendency to sin.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "Deliver me from all my transgressions" [Psalm 39:8]. I have "over-leaped" a great deal of ground, a very great deal of ground already; but, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the Truth is not in us." I have "over-leaped" a great deal: but still do I "beat my breast," and say, "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Thou therefore art "my expectation!" my "End." For "Christ is the end of the Law unto righteousness, unto every man that believeth." From all mine offences: not only from those, that I may not relapse into those which I have already "over-leaped;" but from all, without exception, of those on account of which I now beat my breast, and say, "Forgive us our debts." "Deliver me from all mine offences:" me being thus minded, and holding fast what the Apostle said, "As many of us as be perfect, let us be thus minded." For at the time that he said…
Although this holy man was conducting himself in noble devotion, he still asks to be freed from all of his iniquities by the Lord's mercy.

"From all my iniquities deliver me". He necessarily added "from all", so that of course no iniquity may hold and constrain us. But let us consider how God delivers from iniquities. If, repenting for our evil deeds, we turn to God, God, receiving our conversion from us, grants absolution of iniquities according to the measure of the conversion. For to whom more is remitted, loves more; and therefore it is said of that woman that "much was remitted to her, because she loved much". According to the measure of the repentance, then, the quantity of remission is regulated; let us not deceive ourselves, thinking that these things are dispensed by no rules, by no judgments. For I think that he who has fulfilled all righteousnesses washes away all iniquities; but he who has worked few, or some part of righteousness, dissolves some part of his iniquities; and he who has borne perfect and entire…

"You have made me a reproach to the foolish". As long as we have sins, it is necessary that we be reproached by the foolish one and our accuser, the devil; and if our sins are found not to be blotted out, but written in us by the pen of the devil, through these very things which we have done the enemy will reproach us. For just as all good things are said to be written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, so all evil things are written down with the ink and pen of the devil. On account of which our Lord and Savior blotted out the handwriting of our sins, which was written against us with the devil's endorsement, just as he had also foretold before through the prophet who said: "Behold, I blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist, and I will no longer remember them". Therefore, that we may not be reproached by the foolish one, let us turn ourselves…

"I became dumb;  and I opened not my mouth" [Psalm 39:9]. But it was to guard against "the foolish man," that "I became dumb, and opened not my mouth." For to whom should I tell what is going on within me? "For I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me;  for He will speak peace unto His people."  But "There is no peace," says the Lord, "to the wicked." [Isaiah 48:22] "I was dumb, and opened not my mouth; because it is Thou that made me." Was this the reason that you opened not your mouth, "because God made you"? That is strange; for did not God make your mouth, that you should speak? "He that planted the ear, does He not hear? He that formed the eye, does He not see?"  God has given you a mouth to speak with; and do you say, "I was dumb, and opened not my mouth, because You made me"? Or does the clause, "Because You made me," belong to the verse that follows?

For my part, I realized that this happens to me with your permission, and I waited longer in the knowledge that I would receive help from the same quarter from which comes also the allowance of my suffering.

"I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it is you who did it". This too we have already expounded above, when we treated that verse which says: "While the sinner stands against me, I was struck dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". For it is good that at the time when weapons—whether of disparagements, or of insults, or of reproaches—are hurled against us, we should remember this verse which says: "I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it is you who did it". This indeed seems to need inquiry: what is it that he said, "It is you who did it", and yet did not add what he did. But the very order teaches us, since it describes as a kind of contest between us and the sinner who stands against us; and that it indicates that God did this very thing, that is, that for the sake of our exercise and progress God made these struggles. Therefore for…

The strong hand strikes as though harshly, but it is swift to heal. If it is powerful to wound, it is also powerful when it comes to applying a remedy. As the Lord says, "I will strike, and I will heal." … This hand of the Lord took from Job all that he had and gave it all back again. In fact, he greatly added to Job's store of good things, even doubling what he had before. Do not be troubled because David says he has fainted. A person can faint and rise up stronger than before. "The Lord lifts up all that fall and sets up all that are cast down." Whoever is corrected will rise up with virtue.
source_title: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

quote: "Remove Your stroke away from me" [Psalm 39:10]. Because it is "Thou that hast made me," let it not be Your pleasure to destroy me utterly; scourge, so that I may be made better, not so that I faint; beat me, so that I may be  beaten out to a greater length and breadth, not so that I may be ground to powder. "By the heaviness of Your hand I fainted in corrections." That is, I "fainted" while You were correcting me. And what is meant by "correcting" me? Except what follows.

"Remove your plagues from me; from the strength of your hand I have fainted". What the Latin translators rendered "plagues," in the Greek codices is written "scourges," so that it is: "Remove your scourges from me". This one seems, of course, to say when he is set as it were under the correction of scourges, when, like a man, he is corrected for his sins, or scourged that he may be amended. Just as that also is understood by very many which is written: "Son, do not grow weary of the discipline of God, nor faint when you are rebuked by him. For whom God loves, he corrects, and scourges every son whom he receives". Whenever, therefore, anyone is rebuked with corrections of this kind, he seems fittingly to say: "Remove your scourges from me. From the strength of your hand I have fainted". But that also seems fittingly to be applied which is written: "In rebukes on account of iniquity you…

"Thou with rebukes hast chastened man for iniquity; Thou hast made my life to consume away like a spider" (ver. 11). There is much that is discerned by this Idithun; by every one who discerns as he does; who overleaps as he does. For he says, that he has fainted in God's corrections; and would fain have the stroke removed away from him, "because it is He who made him." Let Him renew me, who also made me; let Him who created me, create me anew. But yet, Brethren, do we suppose that there was no cause for his fainting, so that he wishes to be "renewed," to be "created anew"? It is "for iniquity," saith he, "that Thou hast chastened man." All this, my having fainted, my being weak, my "crying out of the deep," all of this is because of "iniquity;" and in this Thou hast not condemned, but hast "chastened" me. "Thou hast chastened man for sin." Hear this more plainly from another Psalm: "It…

I realize that all your scourging proves to be for a person's correction and betterment; it is not as though you were indifferent to human beings in allowing them to suffer, instead preferring to improve their souls.

"In rebukes for iniquity you have instructed a man, and you have made his soul waste away like a spider". The soul that sins becomes grosser. For such is the nature of sin, on account of which it is written: "The heart of this people has been made gross". But just as sin makes gross, so on the contrary virtue renders the soul subtle, and—if I may wring out, as it were, a novelty of wording—it wipes away and destroys everything corporeal in it, and renders it more purely incorporeal. But that the soul of the sinner grows gross, and, so to speak, becomes fleshly, is indicated by that which is written: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh". Without doubt he names as "flesh" the grosser and sinful souls. If, then, the soul grows gross, so that it becomes flesh, he teaches what remedy God prepares: "In rebukes", he says, "for iniquity you have instructed a man,…

If, then, we turn the discourse back to the nature of that animal, from that aspect by which it unfolds a most subtle work which the eye can scarcely comprehend, the exposition which we explained above will seem apt. But if anyone refers it to that which Isaiah writes in his book, that "they have woven the web of a spider", it is to be taken otherwise: that all the things which the sinner weaves and does, you may know to be as nothing as those things which the spider weaves, though they seem varied and composed, though arranged with a certain exquisite art. How much did those rich men who were before us weave, who gathered riches by various arts and cunning devices, who sought magistracies, honors, consulships with diverse ambition—all these wove the webs of a spider. For as vain, as frivolous as is the weaving of the spider, so were all the things they did, and therefore their souls…

So this is what should concern us, being rescued from sins and attaining reconciliation with you, which results in complete resolution of problems, and not taking pains over other things, which are futile and useless for the painstaker, never bringing one an outcome for the pains or providing one with lasting benefit from the pains.

"Hear my prayer, O Lord" (ver. 12). Whereof shall I rejoice? Whereof should I groan? I rejoice on account of what is past, I groan longing for these which are not yet come. "Hear my prayer, and give ear unto my cry. Hold not Thy peace at my tears." For do I now no longer weep, because I have already "passed by," have "left behind" so great things as these? "Do I not weep much the more?" For, "He that increaseth knowledge, increaseth sorrow." The more I long for what is not here, do I not so much the more groan for it until it comes? do I not so much the more weep until it comes?...

"For I am a sojourner with Thee." But with whom am I a "sojourner"? When I was with the devil, I was a "sojourner;" but then I had a bad host and entertainer; now, however, I am with Thee; but I am a "sojourner" still. What is meant by a sojourner? I am a "sojourner" in the place from which I am to remove;…

What the psalmist means is: As long as I am in this body, I am unhappy. Who of us could say that? If we are octogenarians, we are afraid to die; if we are centenarians and sick besides, still we cling to life and beg for respite. Why do we do that? Because sin gnaws at our conscience. We know that if we leave our body, we are going not to Christ but to hell. On the contrary, what does the apostle say? "I desire to depart and to be with Christ." Give me freedom from anxiety, for after death I am going to be with Christ; even now I long to die. So our psalmist, because he is one who loves the Lord, cries: Unhappy man that I am, because my sojourn is prolonged!

"Hear my prayer, O God, and my supplication; give ear to my tears". It is fitting once again to offer prayer to God even with tears, and to be moved from the innermost recesses into supplication of the Lord, so that the mind, believing in the judgment to come, may review the recollection of its misdeeds not without tears and lamentation. Who, dissolved into tears, says to the Lord: "I pour out my prayer in your sight"? "Give ear, therefore, to my tears, and be not silent", he says, "from me"—that is, while I pray be not silent. But what then? While I am still speaking, say: Behold, I am here.

"For I am a sojourner with you, and a pilgrim, as all my fathers". Because I am a pilgrim, I am necessarily also a sojourner, for I am not as you are. For you alone are eternal, and we, as far as is found, have a beginning. But I, if I be made worthy to be with you, am nevertheless a sojourner and a pilgrim with you; because all my fathers too were sojourners and pilgrims with you; and Abraham is a pilgrim with you, because he did not always exist, but then began to exist when you willed, and so Isaac and Jacob and all the righteous.

Forgive me, so that I need no longer be a pilgrim and a wayfarer. Forgive me so that I may be called home from exile. If you forgive me, before I go from this place, I shall no longer be an exile and a pilgrim. Once you will have forgiven me, I will no longer be in foreign parts. I shall be a fellow citizen of your saints; I shall be with my ancestors, who were pilgrims before me and are now truly citizens. I shall be a member of God's household. I shall not dread punishment but shall merit grace through our Lord Jesus; with whom, Lord God, be praise to you, and honor and glory forever; now and always and for ages of ages. Amen.

quote: "Grant me some remission, that I may be refreshed before I go hence" (ver. 13). Consider well, Idithun, consider what knots those are which thou wouldest have "loosed" unto thee, that thou mightest be "refreshed before thou goest hence." For thou hast certain fever-heats from which thou wouldest fain be refreshed, and thou sayest, "that I may be refreshed," and "grant me a remission." What should He remit, or loosen unto thee, save that difficulty under which, and in consequence of which, thou sayest, "Forgive us our debts. Grant me a remission before I go hence, and be no more." Set me free from my sins, "before I go hence," that I may not go hence with my sins. Remit them unto me, that I may be set at rest in my conscience, that it may be disburthened of its feverish anxiety, the anxiety with which "I am sorry for my sin. Grant me a remission, that I may be refreshed" (before…
Grant me a little time that I may repent for my sins, for in hell no one has the power to confess his sins.

"Give me remission that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more, for I am a sojourner": as long as I am with you, so long I am; but if I go forth from you, I have lost even this very thing that I am, and I shall be as one who is not. Thus for this reason he says concerning sinners: "And they shall be as those who are not". And elsewhere: "Who called the things that are not". "Give me remission that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more". It must be known, nevertheless, that it is within us either to be or not to be. As long as we cleave to God and are joined to him who truly is, we too are. But if we depart from him and do not cleave to our God, we fall by vice into the contrary. Not, therefore, through this is the substantial destruction of the soul designated, but it is said "not to be" when it does not remain in him who truly and always is, from…
